props.title: Samson and Delilah
props.initialSlug: Biblical epic of love, betrayal, and divine strength

sections.content: Cecil B. DeMille's Samson and Delilah (1949) revolutionized Biblical epics with its Technicolor grandeur and provocative mix of sexuality and scripture. Victor Mature's muscular Samson and Hedy Lamarr's seductive Delilah set the template for the sword-and-sandal spectacles that would dominate 1950s Hollywood. The film's massive success paved the way for DeMille's even grander The Ten Commandments (1956) and influenced Biblical adaptations like Quo Vadis (1951) and The Robe (1953). Its lavish costume design by Edith Head won an Oscar and established the glossy, Hollywood look of ancient world epics. The Ten Commandments|1956|DeMille's crowning achievement follows Moses leading the Hebrew exodus from Egypt with groundbreaking effects|Prime Quo Vadis|1951|Peter Ustinov's memorable Nero presides over ancient Rome as Christianity rises, with spectacular set pieces|HBO Max

sections.content: DeMille's approach to Biblical material balanced reverence with entertainment, creating a formula that dominated religious epics for decades. While The Greatest Story Ever Told (1965) attempted a more solemn approach, films like King of Kings (1961) and Solomon and Sheba (1959) followed DeMille's blueprint of mixing spectacle with scripture. The temple destruction sequence in Samson and Delilah particularly influenced later films, with echoes visible in everything from Cleopatra (1963) to modern CGI epics like Exodus: Gods and Kings (2014).

The film's depiction of Delilah established a template for Biblical femmes fatales that influenced later works. Angela Lansbury's Salome in The Story of Mankind (1957) and Rita Hayworth in Salome (1953) built on Lamarr's portrayal of dangerous feminine allure. This tradition extends through Elizabeth Taylor's Cleopatra (1963) and even finds modern expression in films like Noah (2014) and Mary Magdalene (2018). The Robe|1953|Richard Burton stars in this story of the Roman tribune who crucified Jesus and later converts to Christianity|Disney+ SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation and Influence

movies.title: Cleopatra

sections.content: The film's technical achievements were groundbreaking for 1949. Paramount's investment in three-strip Technicolor photography and elaborate practical effects established new standards for Biblical spectaculars. The temple destruction sequence required innovative miniature work that influenced disaster films for decades, visible in films like When Time Ran Out (1980) and even Independence Day (1996). George Pal's later Biblical epic The Story of Ruth (1960) directly borrowed several technical solutions pioneered by DeMille's team.
